name: how-heart-mcp-works
title: heart-mcp: six fixed tools, and the state in every answer
html:
heart-mcp: six fixed tools, and the state in every answer

The model

in any MCP host: Claude Code, Claude Desktop, your agent

chooses the next move

heart-mcp · six tools that never change
heart_lookgo to a bookmark, or read this resource again
heart_acttake one offered act, by name, with fields
heart_followfollow a link, by rel and title
heart_describethe service’s fuller description of an act
heart_explainwhy an act isn’t offered now; nothing is sent
heart_backback one resource, read again
checks the choice: is the act offered? do the fields fit its schema? If not, nothing is sent.

ARTIE, inside

builds every request: address, method, If-Match, credential, L2 forms with integrity checked

→ any HEART service, or the gateway in front of GitHub

Every answer holds

state · the resource’s fields
acts · offered now: name, title, description, schema
links · rel and title
outcome · acted · rejected-before-sending · stale · not-offered · invalid-input · rule-refused

What the model never sees

an address, a method, a header, a validator, a credential

It can’t build a request, and it can’t call an act that isn’t offered.
say: So what would an MCP server look like if it worked like a browser? That's heart-mcp. It gives the model six tools that never change, like a browser's buttons: look, act, follow, describe, explain, back. What changes is what each one answers: the resource's state, the acts offered right now, each with its name, title, description and schema, and the links. The model chooses. heart-mcp checks the choice against what was offered, and against the act's schema, before anything is sent. ARTIE, inside it, builds the request: the address, the method, the If-Match validator, the credential. The model never sees any of those. It can't build a request, and it can't call an act that isn't offered. And when something's off, the outcome says which: acted, rejected before sending, stale, not offered, invalid input, or refused by a rule, in the service's own words. Next, the same thing on real GitHub.
